Stage 6 of 6: Say which worse hands might call or better hands might fold, and compare betting with checking.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

Explain the response a bet needs, then compare checking.

A value-bet explanation needs worse hands that will call. A bluff explanation needs better hands that will fold. A hand's label or one winning result is not a complete reason to bet. Different opposing hands may respond differently.

When the opponent checks to you last to act on the river, checking takes the hand to showdown without a new wager. Compare that option with betting. The frequency of each opposing hand and its response matter, including possible raises.

Both examples use fictional heads-up river hands, ample counters, no fees or side pots and the supplied response assumptions. They teach questions to ask; the site has not measured any player's actual responses.

2. Follow a worked example

The opponent checks to you. Suppose, for this restricted example, a worse pair of nines always folds to your proposed bet and a better hand of three eights always calls. These are two illustrative candidates, not an estimated range.

Your private cards

J♠T♦

Shared river board

T♥8♣5♦3♠2♣

Worse: pair of nines

9♠9♦

Better: three eights

8♠8♦

Your pair of tens beats the nines and loses to three eights. Under these supplied responses, neither candidate supports the proposed value-bet argument: the worse hand does not call, and the better hand does. The better hand does not fold to support a bluff either. Checking already wins against the nines without a new wager. This conclusion is about this restricted model.

3. Explain a changed situation

In a different hand, the opponent checks to you last to act. For a proposed bet of 4, suppose the worse eights call and the better jacks also call. No frequency or complete range has been supplied.

Your private cards

9♥8♥

Shared river board

9♣7♠4♦2♣J♠

Candidate: pair of eights

8♣8♦

Candidate: pair of jacks

J♣T♦

Your task: Which candidate could pay a value bet, and which beats you? What changed from the worked example? What is still missing before saying betting is better than checking?

Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer.

Check your explanation

Your best five are 9-9-J-8-7. The eights are worse and, under the supplied response, call the bet. They are a candidate source of value. The jacks are better and also call, so they cost you when present. Unlike the worked example, at least one worse hand now calls.

That is useful evidence within the example, not a complete verdict. You still need the frequencies of opposing hands, other possible holdings and their responses, including raises. Compare the resulting expectation with checking. Winning one pot would not fill those gaps or prove the bet was best.

Each player receives two private cards, called hole cards. The shared cards form the board: the first three are the flop, the fourth is the turn, and the fifth is the river. A card has a rank , such as an ace or a seven, and a suit : spades, hearts, diamonds or clubs. Aces can be high, or low in an A-2-3-4-5 straight. A pocket pair means your two private cards have the same rank. Suited means they share a suit; offsuit means they do not. Those labels describe useful features, not a decision by themselves. A pair begins with a made pair. Two nearby ranks can work together in straights. Suited cards can work together in flushes. None of that means every pair, connector or suited hand should be played in every situation. Three different starting shapes A pocket pair: two eights. Suited connectors: a jack and ten of hearts. An ace with a lower, offsuit companion. If you see AKs , the final “s” means suited; AKo means offsuit. These are groups of hands, not particular suits. In a full card code such as As , however, “s” means spades. This guide shows the suit symbols and gives each displayed card an accessible full name.

An ace is not a guarantee of a strong hand after the flop. When two players pair the same high card, their other cards can decide the winner. A hand is often called dominated when an opponent shares its higher rank and has a better accompanying card. The weaker hand can improve and still be behind. A pair of aces is not the whole comparison Your cards: Other player's cards: Final board: Before committing chips, identify your position, the price, the effective stack and the action before you. Position tells you who acts before and after you; acting later gives you their actions to consider. In a two-player contest, the effective stack is the smaller relevant stack: with 60 and 100 chips, those players can each contest at most 60 from that point. An unopened pot and a raise followed by a caller are different situations, even when your two cards are identical. Folding is an ordinary option, not a failure to participate. Avoid a rule such as “any ace” or “any two suited cards.” Learn the situation before using a chart. A chart must match the game, stack depth, position and action it describes. The chart-reading guide explains those inputs when you are ready; this lesson does not prescribe a fixed range or bet size.

Your choices depend on the current wager, not just your cards. On a new postflop betting round with no bet yet, you can check or bet . Facing a wager, the usual choices are fold , call or raise , when a raise is permitted and your stack allows it. Short all-ins can create exceptions; ask the dealer when the action is unclear. Three distinctions to say out loud Action What it does Check versus fold Checking keeps your hand in without adding chips when nothing is owed. Folding gives up your claim to the pot. Call versus raise Calling matches the current wager, subject to your stack. Raising increases the wager that others must respond to. Bet versus raise A bet opens wagering on a street. A raise increases an existing wager. The big blind is already a live preflop wager.

The button is a marker identifying the dealer position, even when a staff member deals. The small blind and big blind are forced wagers posted before the cards. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button in preflop action order. At a table with three or more players, preflop action begins clockwise after the big blind. After the flop, action begins with the first remaining player clockwise after the dealer button. Skip folded players and players who are all-in with no chips left to bet. Do not act simply because the player beside you moved: follow the actual order. The big blind has already paid a live wager. If other players only call it, the big blind still gets an option to check or raise. The small blind usually has more to add to complete a call. An ante is a separate contribution and does not reduce the amount owed to a bet. An unraised six-player pot Blinds are 1/2, with no ante or fees. The first two players fold. The cutoff calls 2, the button folds, and the small blind adds 1 to the 1 already posted. The big blind has already posted 2. All players have ample chips. Two-player exception: when the entire table is heads-up, the button is the small blind and acts first preflop, last after the flop. This does not change the positions midway through a hand just because everyone else folded. The position guide develops the difference between a seat and acting after an opponent.

Keep two separate numbers: the current total wager on this street , and what you have already contributed on this street. Their difference is the additional call, unless your remaining stack is smaller. Previous-street contributions are already in the pot and do not pay for a new bet. At a live table, wait until it is your turn and the amount is clear. State your action clearly before moving chips. Do not experiment with silent chip motions: one oversized chip facing a bet is normally a call under TDA procedures, not automatically a raise. The house or tournament rules govern the actual ruling.

A betting round is not finished merely because every player has acted once. A later bet or raise can send the action back around. Players who have not folded and are not all-in must respond to the current wager; everyone entitled to act must have had that opportunity. When all but one player have folded, the hand ends without a showdown. A player who is all-in still has a claim to eligible pots and has not folded. Three players on the flop A checks, B bets 4, C calls 4, and A raises to 12. All three began the street with enough chips to continue. The action goes back to B.

In hold'em, use the best five cards from your two private cards and the five shared cards. You may use two, one or zero private cards. There is no sixth-card tiebreaker, and suits do not break equal hands. This differs from Omaha, which requires exactly two private cards. Preflop means before the first three shared cards appear. Your two private cards have possibilities, not a guaranteed finishing hand. A range is a collection of hands someone could hold or choose to play. Comparing your hand with one imagined opponent hand is different from comparing it with an appropriate range. Hand features to recognize, not a list of automatic plays Feature What to notice A high pair, such as two kings Already a pair, with strength against many unpaired hands. Shared cards and opponents' holdings can still produce a better hand. Two high cards, such as ace-queen Can make high pairs. When an opponent shares your paired rank, kickers can matter. Connected cards, such as jack-ten Can work together in straights. A straight possibility does not guarantee a useful flop or a winning straight. Suited cards Can work together in a flush. A low flush can lose to a higher one. A small pair, such as two fives Already a pair, but higher shared cards can complicate later decisions. A hoped-for third five is not a plan by itself. At a six-player table, the initial preflop order is first to act, the next seat, cutoff, button, small blind and big blind. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button. The cost of calling is what you must add now to match the current wager, subject to your remaining stack. Between two players, the smaller starting stack limits how many starting chips each can contest against the other in this hand. That is their effective starting stack . A small pair may improve to three of a kind, and suited cards may improve to a flush. The possibility of receiving later bets is often discussed as implied odds . Use the same final board and your pair of jacks. You are on the button, only the big blind remains against you, both have chips, and the big blind checks on the river. You act last. The reason “I must bet to stop the flush draw getting there” no longer fits. Checking is unavailable when facing this bet. A player can legally check a strong hand, a medium hand or a hand that is unlikely to win. The rules do not turn a check into an exposed card. A range is not a special ability to see hidden cards. It is a model you can examine and revise. Even a carefully reasoned range can be incomplete or wrong. Return to your king of hearts and queen of diamonds on K♠ 9♣ 5♥ 3♦ 2♣. The king of spades is already on the board, and the king of hearts is in your hand. The opponent cannot hold either card. A value bet aims to get called by a worse hand. A bluff aims to make a better hand fold. These describe an intention relative to the opponent's possible hands, not just the strength of your own two cards. The same pair can be a reasonable value candidate in one assumed situation and an unhelpful bet in another. When no bet is facing you, checking keeps you in the hand without adding chips. Acting last on the river after the opponent checks, your check completes betting and takes the hand to showdown. Checking earlier in the order does not prevent another player from betting. All river comparisons below put you last to act, heads-up, after a check.

One board, four alternative opponents You hold queen of hearts and jack of diamonds: The complete board is queen of spades, eight of clubs, five of hearts, three of diamonds and two of clubs: Your best five are Q-Q-J-8-5 . The pot is 40 before your decision. Both players have 100 behind, with no fees, side pots or tournament payouts. The opponent has checked. A check by you ends betting. We changed the opponent's responses with the price; we did not prove they must behave this way. Raising a pot after a fold can look successful on video. Success at making someone fold is different from getting the most value from a hand. Likewise, losing after a value bet does not automatically invalidate its earlier reasoning. Review the information and assumptions available before the cards were exposed.

A different fictional river You have J♥ T♥, jack-ten of hearts, on K♠ 9♣ 5♥ 3♦ 2♣. The opponent's alternative in this model is Q♥ Q♣. Your K-J-T-9-5 loses to their Q-Q-K-9-5. There are no ties or cards still to come. The pot is 30, both players have 100 behind and the opponent checks to you last to act. The model excludes fees, side pots and raises. Checking loses at showdown. Suppose a bet of 10 makes this better hand fold one quarter of the time and call three quarters of the time. That frequency is supplied for teaching, not measured. Betting a weak hand is not automatically a useful bluff. If you expect only worse hands to fold, those folds do not show that you persuaded a stronger hand to give up. On the river, explain which better hands are the target and what evidence supports their folding. A dramatic single fold cannot establish that frequency.

Move back to the turn Your A♥ J♥ on K♥ 8♥ 3♣ 2♦ has ace high and a heart-flush draw. Against the illustrative K♣ Q♦ it is currently behind a pair of kings. A river 6♥ would make your ace-high flush; a river 7♣ would leave you behind. Neither river is known at the turn decision. Protection , also called denying equity, describes making another hand fold its chance to improve. For example, a pair can benefit when two higher unpaired cards give up before the river. That purpose can overlap with getting worse hands to call. It does not mean that a bet prevents an opponent from calling or guarantees that a made hand stays best. Each player receives two private cards, called hole cards. The shared cards form the board: the first three are the flop, the fourth is the turn, and the fifth is the river. A card has a rank , such as an ace or a seven, and a suit : spades, hearts, diamonds or clubs. Aces can be high, or low in an A-2-3-4-5 straight. A pocket pair means your two private cards have the same rank. Suited means they share a suit; offsuit means they do not. Those labels describe useful features, not a decision by themselves. A pair begins with a made pair. Two nearby ranks can work together in straights. Suited cards can work together in flushes. None of that means every pair, connector or suited hand should be played in every situation. Three different starting shapes A pocket pair: two eights. Suited connectors: a jack and ten of hearts. An ace with a lower, offsuit companion. If you see AKs , the final “s” means suited; AKo means offsuit. These are groups of hands, not particular suits. In a full card code such as As , however, “s” means spades. This guide shows the suit symbols and gives each displayed card an accessible full name.

An ace is not a guarantee of a strong hand after the flop. When two players pair the same high card, their other cards can decide the winner. A hand is often called dominated when an opponent shares its higher rank and has a better accompanying card. The weaker hand can improve and still be behind. A pair of aces is not the whole comparison Your cards: Other player's cards: Final board: Before committing chips, identify your position, the price, the effective stack and the action before you. Position tells you who acts before and after you; acting later gives you their actions to consider. In a two-player contest, the effective stack is the smaller relevant stack: with 60 and 100 chips, those players can each contest at most 60 from that point. An unopened pot and a raise followed by a caller are different situations, even when your two cards are identical. Folding is an ordinary option, not a failure to participate. Avoid a rule such as “any ace” or “any two suited cards.” Learn the situation before using a chart. A chart must match the game, stack depth, position and action it describes. The chart-reading guide explains those inputs when you are ready; this lesson does not prescribe a fixed range or bet size.

Your choices depend on the current wager, not just your cards. On a new postflop betting round with no bet yet, you can check or bet . Facing a wager, the usual choices are fold , call or raise , when a raise is permitted and your stack allows it. Short all-ins can create exceptions; ask the dealer when the action is unclear. Three distinctions to say out loud Action What it does Check versus fold Checking keeps your hand in without adding chips when nothing is owed. Folding gives up your claim to the pot. Call versus raise Calling matches the current wager, subject to your stack. Raising increases the wager that others must respond to. Bet versus raise A bet opens wagering on a street. A raise increases an existing wager. The big blind is already a live preflop wager.

The button is a marker identifying the dealer position, even when a staff member deals. The small blind and big blind are forced wagers posted before the cards. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button in preflop action order. At a table with three or more players, preflop action begins clockwise after the big blind. After the flop, action begins with the first remaining player clockwise after the dealer button. Skip folded players and players who are all-in with no chips left to bet. Do not act simply because the player beside you moved: follow the actual order. The big blind has already paid a live wager. If other players only call it, the big blind still gets an option to check or raise. The small blind usually has more to add to complete a call. An ante is a separate contribution and does not reduce the amount owed to a bet. An unraised six-player pot Blinds are 1/2, with no ante or fees. The first two players fold. The cutoff calls 2, the button folds, and the small blind adds 1 to the 1 already posted. The big blind has already posted 2. All players have ample chips. Two-player exception: when the entire table is heads-up, the button is the small blind and acts first preflop, last after the flop. This does not change the positions midway through a hand just because everyone else folded. The position guide develops the difference between a seat and acting after an opponent.

Keep two separate numbers: the current total wager on this street , and what you have already contributed on this street. Their difference is the additional call, unless your remaining stack is smaller. Previous-street contributions are already in the pot and do not pay for a new bet. At a live table, wait until it is your turn and the amount is clear. State your action clearly before moving chips. Do not experiment with silent chip motions: one oversized chip facing a bet is normally a call under TDA procedures, not automatically a raise. The house or tournament rules govern the actual ruling.

A betting round is not finished merely because every player has acted once. A later bet or raise can send the action back around. Players who have not folded and are not all-in must respond to the current wager; everyone entitled to act must have had that opportunity. When all but one player have folded, the hand ends without a showdown. A player who is all-in still has a claim to eligible pots and has not folded. Three players on the flop A checks, B bets 4, C calls 4, and A raises to 12. All three began the street with enough chips to continue. The action goes back to B.

Preflop means before the first three shared cards appear. Your two private cards have possibilities, not a guaranteed finishing hand. A range is a collection of hands someone could hold or choose to play. Comparing your hand with one imagined opponent hand is different from comparing it with an appropriate range. Hand features to recognize, not a list of automatic plays Feature What to notice A high pair, such as two kings Already a pair, with strength against many unpaired hands. Shared cards and opponents' holdings can still produce a better hand. Two high cards, such as ace-queen Can make high pairs. When an opponent shares your paired rank, kickers can matter. Connected cards, such as jack-ten Can work together in straights. A straight possibility does not guarantee a useful flop or a winning straight. Suited cards Can work together in a flush. A low flush can lose to a higher one. A small pair, such as two fives Already a pair, but higher shared cards can complicate later decisions. A hoped-for third five is not a plan by itself. Several features can combine: jack-ten of hearts is both suited and connected. Features can also come with a weakness: ace-seven offsuit can pair the ace yet lose to a better kicker. Use the worked domination example if that comparison is new. A helpful beginner habit is to describe both an advantage and a vulnerability before declaring a hand “good.” Do not let a suited label excuse every price, or let one memorable win turn a weak situation into a rule.

At a six-player table, the initial preflop order is first to act, the next seat, cutoff, button, small blind and big blind. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button. Some seat labels vary between teaching materials; the number of players and actual action order are the useful facts. For the two scenes below, everyone starts with 100 big blinds before posting, the blinds are 1/2, and there is no ante. Your cards are jack-ten of hearts in both scenes. Nothing about the cards changed. Scene A: You are first to act. All five other players still have their initial decision. Scene B: You are on the button. The first three players folded. Only the two blinds remain to take their initial decision. Being later in the order gives you other players' actions to consider. It does not reveal their private cards. The big blind acts last in the initial preflop order but usually acts before the button after the flop. “Last preflop” and “in position after the flop” are different descriptions. Heads-up has a special order: the button posts the small blind and acts first preflop, then last postflop. See position and stacks for the longer explanation.

An unopened pot has no voluntary call or raise yet: earlier players have folded, or you are first to act. Posting a blind does not count as a voluntary opening raise. A limp is a preflop call of the big blind. An open-raise enters an unopened pot with a raise. Raising after someone has limped is a different situation. A three-bet preflop is a re-raise after that first raise; it does not mean three times the previous amount. For a concrete sequence with blinds 1/2: someone raises to 6, and another player raises to 18. That second raise is a three-bet. A later raise would be a four-bet. “To 18” means a total contribution of 18 on that street, not 18 added on top of an earlier contribution. Same king-queen, different action At a six-player table with blinds 1/2 and no ante, you are the cutoff with king-queen of spades. In scene A, the two earlier players fold. In scene B, the first player raises to 6 and the next calls 6. The button and both blinds are still behind you in either scene. All players began with 200 chips. A chart cell has meaning inside its stated situation, not everywhere those two ranks appear.

The cost of calling is what you must add now to match the current wager, subject to your remaining stack. It is not the total pot, not the opponent's whole stack and not a ticket to see every remaining shared card. Future betting can create new decisions even when your call ends the current round. In these separate six-player scenes, blinds are 1/2 with no ante or fees. The cutoff raises to 6 and the button folds. The earlier players have folded, and everyone has chips left after matching 6. The fraction 4/13 is about 30.8%, but it is not a sufficient preflop calling rule : later betting and how the hand reaches showdown matter. The clean river examples in the pot-odds workshop first remove those complications. A small-looking price and a large-looking pot are prompts to calculate, not reasons to stop thinking.

A stack's chip count becomes more informative when compared with the big blind. For these examples, a starting stack is measured immediately before posting this hand's blind or ante. State that convention in your notes so you do not mix starting chips with chips remaining after bets. Starting stack in BB = starting chips / big blind. The small blind is not the denominator, and a separate ante does not change which number is the big blind. If an ante exists, record it separately because it affects the pot and the situation. Shallower stacks leave less room for later bets relative to the blinds. Deeper stacks create more possible future exposure, not an obligation to commit it. Neither depth guarantees safety or profit. Tournament payouts and remaining players can also affect decisions; a cash-game chart should not silently stand in for a tournament decision near a payout boundary.

Between two players, the smaller starting stack limits how many starting chips each can contest against the other in this hand. That is their effective starting stack . When several players remain, record the separate comparisons. A single number can hide an important deeper opponent. “I cover them” means you have at least as many relevant chips, not that those chips are already yours. If you instead report stacks remaining at a later decision, label the street and contributions already made. Do not compare your remaining stack with an opponent's starting stack as though the numbers describe the same moment.

A small pair may improve to three of a kind, and suited cards may improve to a flush. The possibility of receiving later bets is often discussed as implied odds . The missing word is “if”: if you improve, if your hand is best, and if an opponent contributes more. A deep stack makes more chips available; it does not promise to pay them. Compare two separate scenes: the cutoff began with 14 and now has 8 behind, or began with 200 and now has 194 behind. Both blinds still have a turn. Later costs can move the other way, too. You might make a pair or a low flush, continue paying and lose to a better hand. This is why “I will win a big pot when I hit” needs more than a hopeful ending. Do not substitute a fixed stack multiplier for a full decision without understanding the assumptions behind that shortcut.

Stage 1 of 6: Name your legal actions, count an additional call and build the best five cards.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

Your cards, your turn and your payment are different questions.

Your two private cards belong to you. The board is shared by everyone still in the hand: three cards on the flop, a fourth on the turn and a fifth on the river. On the flop, those five available cards make your current hand. On the turn and river, choose the best five again. At showdown, when all five shared cards are out, you may use zero, one or two private cards.

A check keeps your hand without paying when you owe nothing. A call matches a wager; a raise increases it. Folding gives up your claim to the pot. On your turn facing a bet, with enough chips and raising permitted, you may fold, call or raise. You cannot check past the bet.

Count a call using this betting round only: the current total wager minus what you already paid on this round. Payments on an earlier round stay in the pot. The amount owed says what a call costs, not whether it is a good decision.

2. Follow a worked example

It is your turn on the flop. The opponent bets 4. You have paid nothing on this round and have ample counters. Both short-lesson examples exclude antes, fees and all-ins.

Your private cards

Q♥J♣

Shared flop

Q♠8♦3♠

Your best five are Q-Q-J-8-3: a pair of queens. Calling adds 4 - 0 = 4 counters. You can fold, call 4 or make a legal raise; checking is unavailable. Having a pair does not choose an action for you.

3. Explain a changed situation

A different hand reaches this flop. You paid 6 preflop. The opponent now bets 7; you have paid nothing on this new round. It is your turn, with ample counters and raising permitted.

Your private cards

Q♥J♣

Shared flop

Q♦9♣5♥

Your task: Name your best five. How many additional counters would a call add? Explain whether checking is available and whether the earlier 6 reduces the call.

Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer.

Check your explanation

Your best five are Q-Q-J-9-5, a pair of queens. A call adds 7 - 0 = 7. The 6 was paid preflop and does not pay for a flop bet. Facing this wager, you may fold, call 7 or make a legal raise; you cannot check.

Stage 3 of 6: Name a made hand and a draw separately, then read the action.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

Name the hand you have and the draw you still need.

A made hand describes what your cards make now. A draw describes cards that could improve it. You can have both. A pair needs two cards of one rank; a flush needs five of one suit. Four cards of one suit are not a completed flush.

Count distinct cards, including your private cards and the shared flop. Then describe the action separately. A check does not reveal a weak hand, and a possible improvement does not guarantee the winning hand. These scenes assume it is your turn, ample counters, no all-ins and raising permitted.

2. Follow a worked example

You are on the button. Only you and the big blind reached the flop. The big blind checks to you; nobody has bet on this round.

Your private cards

A♥T♥

Shared flop

T♣7♥2♥

Your best five are T-T-A-7-2: a pair of tens with an ace kicker. There are four hearts, so you also have a heart-flush draw. You may check or bet because nothing is owed. The opponent's check does not tell you which private cards they hold.

3. Explain a changed situation

In another heads-up flop, the opponent bets 5. You have paid nothing on this round.

Your private cards

K♠Q♠

Shared flop

K♦8♠3♠

Your best five are K-K-Q-8-3, a pair of kings with a queen kicker. Four spades give you a spade-flush draw. You may fold, call 5 or make a legal raise; you cannot check past the bet.

Stage 5 of 6: Separate known cards, possible opposing hands and assumptions about their frequency.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

A possible hand is different from a likely hand.

A range is a model of the hands an opponent could hold in a situation. First remove exact cards you already know. A card cannot be in your private hand, on the board and in an opponent's hand at the same time.

Then separate possibility from frequency. A legal holding may be possible without being common. A check is an observed action; the cards and frequencies behind it remain uncertain. Listing three candidates does not give each a one-third chance, and these candidate lists are not complete ranges.

2. Follow a worked example

The opponent checks to you on the river. Consider the three exact candidate holdings below.

Your private cards

A♥T♦

Shared river board

T♠8♣5♥3♦2♠

Candidate A

A♥K♥

Candidate B

A♣K♦

Candidate C

T♥T♣

A is impossible: it reuses your ace of hearts. B is physically possible, but its frequency is unknown. C is also possible and makes three tens, which beat your pair. Checking therefore does not prove the opponent holds a weaker hand. None of these observations supplies probabilities.

3. Explain a changed situation

In another river hand, the opponent checks. Consider these different exact candidates.

Your private cards

K♠Q♥

Shared river board

Q♠9♦6♣4♠2♥

Candidate A

K♠J♥

Candidate B

K♥K♣

Candidate C

J♦T♦

Your task: Which candidate is impossible? Can a legal candidate beat your queens? Does a candidate being legal, or appearing once at showdown, establish how often it checks?

Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer.

Check your explanation

A is impossible because you hold the king of spades. B and C reuse none of the known cards. B makes a pair of kings and beats your queens; C does not. A check is compatible with either legal holding.

Neither physical possibility nor one reveal establishes a frequency. Different models can allow the same observed hand. Say which cards and actions are known, then label any frequency as an assumption needing evidence.

Stage 2 of 6: Describe position and earlier action before judging two private cards.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

Read the action before deciding what two cards mean.

The button marks the dealer position. At a table of three or more players, preflop action starts after the big blind and proceeds clockwise. In a six-player game, the initial order is first seat, next seat, cutoff, button, small blind, big blind. The cutoff is the seat immediately before the button.

After the flop, the first remaining player clockwise after the button acts first. The button therefore acts after a blind on the flop, but the blinds still have initial turns after the button preflop. A later raise can give earlier players another decision.

Describe your seat, earlier action, price and relevant stacks before using a hand label or chart. Suited means your two cards share a suit; it does not establish that playing them is best. These examples use six players who began with 100 counters each, blinds 1/2 and no ante or fees.

2. Follow a worked example

The first seat, next seat and cutoff fold. You are on the button with queen-jack of spades. The small blind has posted 1 and the big blind 2. Neither blind has taken its initial turn.

Your private cards

Q♠J♠

You face an unraised big blind. A call would add 2 because you have paid zero. Both blinds still have decisions after your initial action; either may raise. Being on the button does not finish preflop. This description does not prescribe a call or a raise.

3. Explain a changed situation

You now sit in the small blind with the same private cards. The first two seats fold, the cutoff raises to 6, and the button calls 6. Your posted small blind is 1. The big blind has not yet acted.

Your private cards

Q♠J♠

Your task: How much more would your call add? Who still has an initial decision after you? Explain two ways this situation differs from the worked example, despite the same private cards.

Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer.

Check your explanation

A call adds 6 - 1 = 5. The big blind still has an initial decision, and a raise could return action to you or the earlier players. The pot has already been raised and called, and you are in the small blind rather than on the button.

Your two cards did not change, but the earlier action, price and position did. If you reach a flop, the small blind acts before the other remaining seats in this six-player hand. The price alone does not settle whether to continue.

Stage 4 of 6: Rebuild the best five after each new card and distinguish a call price from a reason to call.

Work through this short lesson, then pause or continue. The full explanation and other practice are available below.

1. Learn one idea

Rebuild the hand, then price the call without inventing its chances.

The turn is the fourth shared card; the river is the fifth and last. Rebuild your best five when a card arrives. A missed draw can leave a pair, but no later community card can complete a draw once the river is out.

For a heads-up river call that ends betting, the break-even pot share in chips is the additional call divided by the pot after your call. This is a price. Your expected share against possible opposing hands, including ties, is a different question.

Both scenes assume a fictional cash game, ample chips, no fees, no side pots and no tournament payout effects. A fold or legal raise may also be available; pricing a call does not compare every action.

2. Follow a worked example

The opponent bets 12 into a river pot of 24. You have paid nothing on this round.

Your private cards

J♥T♥

Shared river board

J♣8♥3♥2♦5♠

Your best five are J-J-T-8-5. The heart draw missed; you still have a pair of jacks. The bet makes the current pot 36. Calling adds 12 and makes 48, so 12 / 48 = 25% is the break-even share. It is not a measured chance that your hand wins.

3. Explain a changed situation

A different river pot contains 36 before the opponent bets 12. You have paid nothing on the river; a call ends betting under the same assumptions.

Your private cards

Q♠J♠

Shared river board

Q♥9♠4♠2♣6♦

Your task: List the best five. Did the spade draw arrive? Give the current pot, the pot after calling and the break-even share. What is still missing before recommending a call?

Say your explanation or write it on paper before opening the answer.

Check your explanation

Your best five are Q-Q-J-9-6. Four spades leave a missed flush draw and a pair of queens. The current pot is 48; your additional 12 makes 60. The break-even share is 12 / 60 = 20%.

The same bet of 12 has a different price because the earlier pot changed. You still need a justified model of the opponent's possible hands and their frequencies to estimate your pot share, including ties. The arithmetic alone does not show that calling is best.
